prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Grandma is washing me white. I am the color of hot sand in the bleached sea light. I am a stain on the porcelain, persistent as tea. Stay in the shade. Don’t say she was the only one. Cousins opposite say: you too white. I am a night-blooming flower being pried open in the morning. My skin a curtain for a cage of bones, a blackbird coop. My heart is crusty bread, hardening. Hardening. This way, I feed my own fluttering. Under shade, the day looks like evening and I cannot bear the darkness. Don’t say, I can’t stand to be touched. Say, I stare into the sun to burn off the soiled hands that print my body with bloody ink. Don’t say, Mulatto. Say, I am the horse in Oz turning different colors, each prance brightening flesh. A curiosity. Don’t say, Bathwater spiraled down into the pipes. Say, I never did fade. Say, Skin holds the perseverance of my days. Folding, folding, the water continuously gathers, making wrinkles in a map.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker grapples with colorism and conflicting judgments about being too dark or too white.
- The speaker experiences their body and skin as sites of pain, scrutiny, and imposed meaning.
- The text rejects harmful labels and silences by replacing them with more self-defined language.
- The speaker insists that their identity has not faded despite attempts to wash, mark, or redefine them.
- The speaker presents skin as a record of endurance, memory, and survival.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Grandma, Stay, Don

outputs.L1:
Grandma is washing me white. I am the color of hot sand in bleached sea light. I am a stain on porcelain, persistent as tea.

Stay in the shade.

Don’t say she was the only one.

Cousins opposite say: you too white.

I am a night-blooming flower pried open in morning. My skin, a curtain drawn over a cage of bones, a blackbird coop. My heart is crusted bread, hardening. Hardening. In this way, I feed my own fluttering.

Under shade, the day looks like evening, and I cannot bear the darkness.

Don’t say, I can’t stand to be touched.

Say, I stare into the sun to burn away the soiled hands that print my body in bloody ink.

Don’t say, Mulatto.

Say, I am the horse in Oz turning different colors, each prance brightening flesh. A curiosity.

Don’t say, Bathwater spiraled down into the pipes.

Say, I never did fade.

Say, Skin holds the perseverance of my days. Folding, folding, the water gathers continuously, making wrinkles in a map.
outputs.L2: Grandmother scrubs me toward whiteness. My body is the shade of sun-scorched sand under the ocean’s pale glare. Against the porcelain, I remain like a mark that will not lift, as stubborn as tea. Keep out of the sun. Do not claim she was alone in this. Relatives on the other side tell me: you are too pale. I am a flower meant to open at night, forced apart in daylight. My skin hangs like fabric over a barred house of bones, a pen for blackbirds. My heart is stale bread, growing tougher. Tougher. In this way, I nourish the wings inside me. In the shadows, afternoon resembles dusk, and I cannot endure that dimness. Do not say I hate being handled. Say I look straight into the sun, trying to scorch away the dirty hands that have stamped my body in blood-dark ink. Do not say “mulatto.” Say I am the color-changing horse from Oz, every step making my flesh shine differently. A spectacle. Do not say the bathwater twisted away through the plumbing. Say I did not disappear. Say my skin carries the endurance of all my years. Creasing again and again, the water keeps collecting, drawing folds like lines across a map.
outputs.L3:
The speaker grapples with the painful realities of colorism and the contradictory judgments placed upon their identity. They are made to feel as though they are always being measured against impossible standards: too dark for some, too white for others, never allowed simply to exist as they are. These judgments reveal how skin color becomes a site of social conflict, where others attempt to define belonging, authenticity, and worth through appearance.

Throughout the text, the speaker experiences their body and skin as places where pain, scrutiny, and imposed meaning gather. Their skin is not treated as neutral or ordinary; instead, it becomes something that others read, criticize, mark, and misunderstand. The body carries the weight of outside assumptions, becoming a surface onto which prejudice, shame, and expectation are projected.

However, the text also resists these harmful interpretations. Rather than accepting labels that diminish or silence them, the speaker pushes back by choosing language that is more self-defined and empowering. They reject names, judgments, and categories that have been used to wound them. In doing so, they reclaim the right to describe themselves on their own terms.

The speaker also insists that their identity has not disappeared, even though others have tried to wash it away, mark it, or redefine it. Attempts to erase or alter who they are have not succeeded. Their sense of self remains present and intact, despite the pressure to conform to other people’s ideas of race, beauty, or belonging.

Ultimately, the speaker presents skin as more than a physical surface. It becomes a record of endurance, memory, and survival. Their skin holds the evidence of what they have lived through, including pain and resilience. Rather than being a source of shame, it becomes a testament to their continued existence and strength.
outputs.L4:
The text explores how racialized colorism shapes the speaker’s sense of self, using images of the body, skin, and speech to reveal the damage caused by shame. It presents skin not as a simple physical surface, but as a place where history, judgment, and memory are written. Through lyrical imagery, the speaker suggests that color has been treated as something to measure, criticize, or correct. This creates a painful tension between how the speaker is seen by others and how the speaker understands the self.

A central part of the text is its use of negation: the repeated attention to what should not be said, what should not be believed, and what should not be allowed to define the body. These refusals challenge the language of insult and erasure that has been placed on darker skin. Instead of accepting the idea that darkness is a mark of shame, the text reframes it as evidence of presence, inheritance, and survival. The speaker resists the terms that others have used to diminish them and begins to transform those meanings.

The text also focuses on violated identity. The speaker’s body has been made into a site of public judgment, as though it belongs to other people’s opinions rather than to the self. This violation is not only physical but emotional and linguistic: harm happens through words, comparisons, silence, and the pressure to disappear. Yet the speaker’s voice pushes back against that harm. By naming what has been done, the text refuses to let shame remain hidden or unquestioned.

Ultimately, the statement that the speaker “never did fade” becomes an act of defiance and self-affirmation. It rejects the idea that the speaker’s skin is a stain, a flaw, or something to be erased. Instead, skin becomes a record of endurance, carrying the evidence of survival through generations of violence, colorism, and rejection. The body that others tried to shame is reclaimed as proof of persistence. In this way, the text turns pain into witness and transforms the speaker’s skin into a symbol of lasting strength.
outputs.L5:
Grandma always knew how to make a house feel like home. Whenever Don came to visit, she would meet him at the door with a warm smile and the smell of fresh bread drifting from the kitchen.

“Stay a little longer,” Grandma would say, patting the chair beside her. Don never needed much convincing. He loved listening to her stories about the old days, about the garden she planted every spring, and about the little moments that made life meaningful.

As the evening grew quiet, Don realized that Grandma’s house was more than a place to visit. It was a place where time slowed down, where memories lived, and where love always asked you to stay.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a mixed-race speaker reflecting on childhood colorism, being scrubbed by a grandmother, and reclaiming their skin, using fragmented “Don’t say / Say” refrains.
counterfactuals.output:
Don’t say dirty.  
Say earth remembering rain.

My grandmother held my wrist beneath the faucet like a question she already knew the answer to. Warm water, white soap, the hard moon of her knuckles. She scrubbed and scrubbed as if dusk were a thing I had rolled in, as if the brown of me were mischief, stain, proof of a door left open too long. I was small enough to believe the body could apologize.

Don’t say too dark.  
Say the room needed more night.

In the mirror I learned fractions before numbers: half this, half that, not enough of either to be whole. The cousins lined up like paint chips, praised in the language of milk and peach and “good hair.” I stood beside them, a storm cloud with knees, while the aunties hummed their weather reports. Pretty, but. Smart, but. Such big eyes, but. Their buts built a fence around my face.

Don’t say lucky to be light.  
Say history makes bargains with children.

Grandmother loved me with the terror she inherited. Her hands were not cruel at first; they were afraid. Afraid of sun. Afraid of men with clipboards, women with pursed mouths, classrooms where names were mispronounced into cages. She had survived by polishing herself toward permission. So she polished me. Behind her, generations gathered with their washcloths, whispering, If we can make the child gleam, perhaps the world will not bite.

Don’t say she meant well.  
Say love can carry a blade and not know it is bleeding you.

The soap foamed gray at the sink. See? she said. See what comes off? I looked at the water and thought I was leaving myself there, circling the drain in small brown galaxies. I wanted to be held without correction. Wanted a towel soft as yes. Wanted someone to say, This is your gold. This is your bark. This is the shore where your mother and father met and made a sunrise no one gets to rename.

Don’t say exotic.  
Say I am not a country you discovered.

Don’t say caramel, coffee, spice.  
Say my skin without eating it.

Don’t say mixed like confusion.  
Say mixed like choir, like river mouth, like two languages kissing in my blood.

Years later, I bathe slowly. No one stands over me. The cloth in my hand is only a cloth. I wash the day from my shoulders and keep the dusk. I oil my arms until they shine with their own weather. I press my palms to my cheeks, my knees, my belly, all the places I was taught to revise, and I do not revise them. I call each shade by its secret name: cedar, amber, clay after thunder, honey in a dark jar, my grandmother’s shadow, my father’s summer, my mother’s lamp.

Don’t say stain.  
Say inheritance.

Don’t say scrub.  
Say ceremony.

Don’t say shame.  
Say old ghost, you may leave now.

And when the mirror asks its ancient question, I answer with my whole unbleached body. I answer in pigment. I answer in the brown that stayed. I answer in the child rising from the sink, slick with soap, bewildered and holy, reaching for my hand across all these years.

Come here, I tell them.  
Come here, beloved.

Don’t say clean.  
Say free.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental first-person poem in the style of contemporary confessional prose poetry about skin tone, family shame, bathing, and survival, with vivid surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
I learned my color in the bathroom, under the jaundiced bulb, where water made a small country of my knees.

My mother said scrub, and handed me the cloth like a verdict. My aunties whispered in the hallway with their mouths full of moths. Dark girl. Sun girl. Too-much-of-the-outside girl. I stood in the tub and watched soap gather in the hollow of my throat, a white animal pretending to save me.

I rubbed until my arms reddened into another kind of shame.

The water ran brown with dirt, they said, but I knew the drain was swallowing a little family history each time: the field, the border, the grandmother who never learned to say beautiful without lowering her voice. Our house kept a jar of silence beside the sink. We used it for everything. Wounds. Weddings. Photographs where my face was turned toward the flash like an apology.

Once, I dreamed my skin unzipped itself and stepped out of me, dripping and furious. It sat on the toilet lid, crossed its legs, and smoked one of my father’s cigarettes. You want to be clean? it asked. Clean like bone? Clean like the plate after everyone has eaten?

I woke with the taste of metal and rain in my mouth.

In the bath, I became an experiment: lemon, milk, prayer, cheap bleach creams hidden behind the towels. I became a rumor my relatives tried to correct. I became the girl who wore long sleeves in summer, who smiled with all her teeth at cousins pale as uncooked rice. I became the mirror’s stubborn weather.

But survival is also a kind of bathing.

Now I lower myself into water and do not ask permission. I let my body cloud the tub with its living. I soap the places I was taught to hate: elbow, thigh, neck, the small dark moons of my knuckles. I call each one by its secret name. I say inheritance. I say earth after rain. I say the night is not an insult.

My shame floats up around me in gray ribbons, then changes—eel, smoke, black silk, my mother’s hair. I do not drain it right away. I watch it shimmer. I watch it learn to be beautiful without disappearing.

When I rise, the mirror fogs over like a witness refusing to testify.

I press my palm to the glass.

On the other side, someone presses back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic monologue from the perspective of someone whose grandmother tried to wash their skin lighter, exploring trauma, touch, and identity without using straightforward explanation.
counterfactuals.output:
She called it care.

A basin in the kitchen,  
blue plastic, split at the rim,  
filled with warm water and the sharp white moon  
of soap.

Her hands were small birds,  
but they came at me like weather.

Scrub, she would say—  
not to me, exactly,  
to the shadow she believed had settled  
too deep in the grain.

The cloth rasped circles into my arms,  
my knees,  
the brown hills of my shoulders.  
Foam gathered there  
like a prayer that had forgotten  
who it was praying for.

I learned early  
that touch could arrive wearing an apron,  
smelling of lavender and lye,  
humming hymns through clenched teeth.

I learned the body can become a house  
where someone keeps opening windows  
to let the wrong thing out.

Grandmother,  
your love had knuckles.

It shone silver in the tub,  
it wrung itself dry over the line,  
it folded me into towels  
and searched for a paler child  
inside the steam.

But I was never under there.

Not beneath the suds,  
not beneath the sting,  
not beneath the red bloom rising  
where the cloth had argued with my skin.

I was the dark water left behind,  
warm with myself.

I was the stain that would not confess.

Now, when rain touches me,  
I flinch—  
then listen.

The sky has softer hands than we were given.  
It does not ask my face to change.  
It beads on my cheek  
like small black seeds,  
like names returned from burial.

I stand in the mirror  
and gather every shade she tried to loosen:  
molasses, walnut, wet earth after thunder,  
the deep brown throat of a cello,  
the holy underside of bark.

I wear them all.

Some nights I still feel her  
working at my wrists,  
as if my pulse were a stubborn mark  
on the linen of her world.

And I want to tell her—  
the river does not apologize  
for carrying silt.

The night does not kneel  
to become dawn.

A girl is not a mistake  
because the room was taught  
to fear its own darkness.

Grandmother,  
I have stopped rinsing.

I let the old water go cold.

I step out  
gleaming with what stayed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, metaphor-rich prose poem that includes images of porcelain, tea stains, shade, cousins commenting on skin color, a night-blooming flower, blackbirds, Oz’s color-changing horse, and bathwater spiraling away.
counterfactuals.output: Porcelain remembers every hand that lifted it: the cup, the sink, the saintly basin chipped at the rim, all of them pretending whiteness is innocence and not merely clay held too long in fire. In my grandmother’s kitchen, tea stains bloomed like old maps at the bottom of cups, small brown continents no one would name, while the cousins leaned in with their sugared mouths and said, You got darker this summer, said it like weather, like warning, like shade was something I had stolen and worn. Outside, the shade gathered under the guava tree in a velvet congregation, and the blackbirds stitched themselves through it, sharp needles of hunger and song. By evening, the night-blooming flower loosened its pale throat, opening only when the world stopped asking it to be seen, pouring out a sweetness so heavy it seemed almost bruised. I thought then of Oz’s color-changing horse, that miraculous animal washed from one hue into another as if identity were a stable with rainbow doors, as if a body could be rinsed clean of rumor, family, sun. But in the bathroom, the porcelain tub held me plainly; the water darkened with the day, with dust, with the invisible ink of being looked at. When the plug was pulled, bathwater spiraled away in a small obedient galaxy, taking nothing it promised to take, leaving the ring, the stain, the skin, the night flower breathing in the yard, and the blackbirds, blackbirds, blackbirds, signing their names across the last light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short literary piece about colorism and the word “mulatto,” structured around rejecting harmful phrases and replacing them with empowering images of endurance and unfading skin.
counterfactuals.output:
Don’t call me **mulatto**.

Do not make my body a footnote to conquest,  
a fraction measured in someone else’s mouth.  
Do not call my skin a question,  
a compromise,  
a stain trying to explain itself.

Say instead:  
I am clay that remembers the river.  
I am dusk holding the sun without apology.  
I am the brown of bread, earth, bark, and drum—  
not half of anything,  
but whole with every ancestor still breathing.

Do not say **good hair**  
as if my coils are guilty.  
Say crown.  
Say storm-root.  
Say black vine reaching for sky.

Do not say **too dark**  
as if night has ever begged permission to be beautiful.  
Say velvet.  
Say fertile ground.  
Say the place where stars learn to shine.

Do not say **almost white**  
like whiteness is a door I should thank for opening.  
Say unbleached.  
Say unbought.  
Say skin that did not fade when the world tried to rinse it clean.

I am not the bruise of two histories colliding.  
I am the scar that learned to sing.  
I am pigment with a pulse.  
I am endurance, unfading—  
melanin like memory,  
skin like flame that refuses to dim.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
